5247.dq: Citation forms of single words elicited/agreed in community orthography workshops with elder speakers; IPA transcriptions with primary-stress mark; appendix basic wordlist (pp.52-69) carries acute/circumflex stress marks on most items. Note 'tono' in the Inata-language column means 'sound' (tunog), not lexical tone; no tone is described.
5247.prule: Word stress (diin) is contrastive in Inata: it falls on either the penultimate or the final syllable as a lexical property, independent of a word-final glottal stop, giving the four Philippine-style classes malumay (penult stress, no final glottal: maáju, garányon), mabilis (final stress: sapót, kansiyón), malumi (penult stress + final glottal: aniyà, tubò) and maragsa (final stress + final glottal: bitû, sapâ, amâ, inâ); stress alone distinguishes words (yusóng vs yúsong, bugsók vs búgsok), and the orthography marks the stressed vowel with an acute (circumflex when the stressed final syllable also ends in a glottal stop).

5249.dq: like all the other dialects of B 40, except Ngubi, ɣi-Sirə is a so-called "tone-case" language, a misleading expression which should be taken to mean that the tone-pattern of a nominal varies according to its position in the utterance though not necessarily according to its grammatical function.
5249.dloc: pp. 18-19, §2 (tone-case statement, said of ɣi-Sirə and 'all the other dialects of B 40, except Ngubi')
5249.prule: Varama has lexical tone of the B40 type: nominals fall into tone-classes A/B/C/D (underlying °LL, °HL, °LH, °HH, reflexes of Proto-Bantu *LL/*HL/*LH/*HH), established in a post-verbal test frame; an older speaker still separates D1 (<*HH) from D2 (<*HL) by a slight tonal difference, a younger speaker has merged them; as in the rest of B40 (except Ngubi) the surface tone pattern of a nominal varies with its position in the utterance ('tone-case'). Stress not discussed in the source.

5254.prule: Not a rule for the language: Geary interprets the acute accent marks that Hariot/White wrote on some 1585-88 Carolina Algonquian words. Reading them through Fox (Meskwaki) prosody, he takes most of them to mark a high pitch-accent on the syllable that was the Proto-Algonquian antepenult (= the penult of the attested, apocopated form), followed by a falling accent on the old penult (attested ultima); for other words he says the mark sits 'where there should be a stress-accent'. His global verdict: Hariot's accents are pitch-accents, not stress-accents. Word-level prominence itself is never described first-hand; no speaker was ever heard by a linguist.

5267.prule: Word stress is predominantly initial: disyllables are almost always stressed on the first syllable; four-syllable words usually carry accents on the first and third syllables (alternating rhythm; which of the two carries the main accent is marked per item — e.g. o e moerinam 'index finger' on the first, atem i e rim 'middle finger' on the third — not stated as a rule); trisyllables vary between initial and second-syllable (medial) stress, item by item. qtr.text: Tonal realization rules generate these surface tonal units from underlying representations in which only two tonemes figure: high and low. 5272.dq: Statement is about lexical (word-level) underlying tone schemes and sentence-level realization rules; data are sentences from one speaker (Mamadou Kanté, Wèdala, Dec 1983). grep over the OCR for accent/intensité/proéminence/stress: no occurrence -> no word-stress statement either way.
5272.prule: Koro (korokan) is a tone language: two underlying tonemes H and L; lexical tone schemes H / L(h) for monosyllables, HH / LH / LL(h) for disyllables, HHH/LHH/LLH for trisyllables, every lexeme must contain at least one final H (possibly floating); surface contours derive via tonal compactness, floating-H deletion, flattening of rising schemes, and Koro-specific rightward spreading of both H and L (rules R1-R11), yielding downstepped H and HL contour tones; the definite marker is a floating L+H. Nothing is said about word stress/accent.

5273.dq: Statement concerns the tonal notation of word and sentence data in Zwernemann's documents (isolated words and short sentences); it is a report about the source's transcription (2 levels), not an analysis of the tone system; no word-stress claim either way.
5273.prule: Second-hand: the only primary source (Zwernemann 1996) transcribes Kpeen with two tone levels (H marked acute, L marked grave, as in the quoted examples ná tɔ́ nè, mwɔ̀ sí à ná ná nè); Idiatov treats Kpeen as a tone language like its Samogo sisters (Dzuun, Ban 3 levels; Jo, Seen 4) but flags the two-level notation as possibly under-analysed. Stress not discussed in the source.
